definition: The energy of the random jiggling motion of atoms and molecules in a material.
A measure of how vigorous the random atomic motion is on average; at 300 K the typical thermal energy scale is k_B T, about 0.026 eV.
Energy in transit from one object to another because of a temperature difference, moved by conduction, convection, or radiation.
The continuous spectrum of electromagnetic waves emitted by every object above absolute zero because its randomly moving charges accelerate.
An ideal object that absorbs all radiation hitting it; it is also the best possible emitter, and its spectrum depends only on its temperature.
The formula (1900) giving a blackbody's brightness at each wavelength for a given temperature; deriving it required assuming energy comes in chunks of hf.
The peak wavelength of a blackbody's spectrum is 2898 micrometer-kelvins divided by its temperature, so hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths.
The total power radiated by a surface is P = emissivity x sigma x area x T^4, so doubling the absolute temperature multiplies the power by 16.
A number from 0 to 1 giving how well a surface emits thermal radiation compared with a blackbody; shiny metals are about 0.02-0.05, skin and matte black paint about 0.95-0.98.
At each wavelength a surface's emissivity equals its absorptivity: good absorbers are good emitters, and good reflectors are poor emitters.
About 798 K (525 degrees C), the temperature at which a hot object's dull red glow first becomes visible in the dark.
The temperature of a blackbody whose glow has the same color as a given light source; warm-white bulbs are about 2700 K, daylight about 5000-6500 K.
Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths from about 0.7 micrometers to 1 millimeter, longer than red light; everyday objects emit mostly in the thermal infrared near 10 micrometers.
A thermal-camera pixel that warms slightly when infrared lands on it, changing its electrical resistance; most such cameras work in the 8-14 micrometer band.
The 8-13 micrometer band where air absorbs little thermal infrared, letting Earth's surface radiate directly to space and letting thermal cameras see through air.
Warming of Earth's surface because gases such as CO2 and water vapor pass incoming sunlight but absorb and re-emit outgoing thermal infrared, some of it back downward.
Heating by an oscillating electric field that twists polar molecules such as water; because the molecules lag behind the field, energy is lost into random motion. It is how microwave ovens work.
Spacecraft blankets made of many thin aluminized plastic layers separated by vacuum, which block heat flow by radiation.
A panel with a high-infrared-emissivity (often white) coating that rejects waste heat to space by thermal radiation, the only cooling route available in vacuum.
Straw, brown, purple, and blue colors on steel heated to about 200-350 degrees C, caused by thin-film interference in a growing oxide layer, not by glowing.
